definition: Computer audition (CA) or machine listening is the general field of study of algorithms and systems for audio interpretation by machines.
details: Since the notion of what it means for a machine to "hear" is very broad and somewhat vague, computer audition attempts to bring together several disciplines that originally dealt with specific problems or had a concrete application in mind. The engineer Paris Smaragdis, interviewed in Technology Review, talks about these systems — "software that uses sound to locate people moving through rooms, monitor machinery for impending breakdowns, or activate traffic cameras to record accidents." Inspired by models of human audition, CA deals with questions of representation, transduction, grouping, use of musical knowledge and general sound semantics for the purpose of performing intelligent operations on audio and music signals by the computer. Technically this requires a combination of methods from the fields of signal processing, auditory modelling, music perception and cognition, pattern recognition, and machine learning, as well as more traditional methods of artificial intelligence for musical knowledge representation.

explainer.lead: Computer audition, also called machine listening, studies how computers can interpret sound and music. It matters because audio can reveal useful events, such as someone moving through a room, machinery approaching a breakdown, or an accident that should trigger a traffic camera.

tiers.eli5: Computer audition is like teaching a computer to be a careful listener. A mechanic might notice that a machine sounds wrong before it breaks; a listening computer tries to notice useful clues in sounds too. It can then do something with what it hears, such as finding where a person is or switching on a camera.
tiers.practitioner: An engineer typically combines signal processing with auditory modelling, pattern recognition, and machine learning to turn audio into an interpretation. Music applications may also require music perception, cognition, and representations of musical knowledge. A key pitfall is treating machine listening as only a classification problem when representation, transduction, grouping, or sound semantics also need attention.
tiers.paperLevel: Computer audition can be written as CA: audio or music signals -> intelligent operations, using representations and models of sound together with computational inference. Its methods draw on signal processing, auditory modelling, music perception and cognition, pattern recognition, machine learning, and artificial-intelligence techniques for musical knowledge representation. The field has no single narrow notion of machine hearing, so its scope and system requirements vary with the interpretation task.

explainer.example: A machinery-monitoring system receives the sound of equipment while it operates. It processes that audio to identify indications of an impending breakdown, producing a warning so the machine can be checked.

explainer.intuition: Human listening involves more than detecting that a sound exists: it involves organizing sounds and connecting them to meaning. Computer audition similarly aims to turn audio into useful interpretations and actions.
howItWorks: A system processes audio or music signals and builds representations that support operations such as grouping and interpretation. Depending on the task, it combines signal processing, auditory models, pattern recognition, machine learning, and knowledge about music or sound semantics.
explainer.whyItMatters: Sound carries information that can support monitoring, localization, and automatic responses without relying only on visual input. Computer audition provides a common field for techniques that were originally developed for separate audio problems and applications.
misconceptions: It is not one single listening algorithm.
It is not limited to music signals.
It involves interpretation, not just recording audio.
It does not depend on machine learning alone.
